name: ccache
baseline: Uncached compilation (same compiler command run without ccache); the page does not involve Make/Ninja and does not name the compiler
workload: Median of 100 runs compiling ccache's own ccache.c (-g -O2 -MD) and a preprocessor-heavy c++_includes.cc (-MD), comparing no-cache vs ccache's direct/preprocessor/depend cache-hit modes.
claimed_speedup: ccache.c: 145.39x (direct mode), 137.81x (depend mode), 28.33x (preprocessor mode) vs no cache. c++_includes.cc: 29.10x (direct), 29.32x (depend), 5.09x (preprocessor) vs no cache.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not named on page; -g -O2 -MD plus needed -I flags (ccache.c); -MD only (c++_includes.cc); ccache 3.7.1
hardware: Intel Core i5-4690K, standard SSD, Linux desktop
stars_or_usage: 3.0k stars; bundled/used by default in many Linux distro and CI C/C++ build pipelines
tradeoffs: Only accelerates cache-hit rebuilds; provides no benefit on true cold/clean builds; requires stable compiler/flags/includes for hits; direct mode is disabled by some preprocessor macros (e.g. __TIME__).
caveats: Measures single-file cache hits against a plain uncached compile, not an end-to-end Make/Ninja build, so real speedup depends on hit rate. Cache misses are slower than no cache: first-time runs were 0.96-0.98x (ccache.c) and 0.83-0.97x (c++_includes.cc), and the page cites 5-20% miss overhead (1-3% in depend mode). The page does not name the compiler or give a date. It was measured with the old ccache 3.7.1 on a dated i5-4690K. ccache is itself a named baseline of the compile-caching-and-distribution category.

name: Bazel
baseline: GNU Make 4.3 with default built-in rules (also measured: Make with --no-builtin-rules --no-builtin-variables, and Ninja 1.11.1, both of which beat Bazel)
workload: Third-party overhead benchmark: N simulated modules (50 to 100,000) whose build rules only touch 0-byte files, measured as full build, incremental build (one most-imported interface file rewritten) and null build (nothing changed), parallelism 4, one run per cell.
claimed_speedup: Bazel's own README claims only 'fast and incremental builds' (no numbers). Third-party table, x86_64, 100,000 modules: incremental build Bazel 61.911 s vs recursive Make (default rules) 692.201 s and single Make 292.019 s (about 11x and 4.7x, derived from page data); null build Bazel 20.193 s vs 688.101 s and 285.583 s (about 34x and 14x, derived from page data). At 5,000 modules: incremental 4.040 s vs 22.408 s / 24.813 s; null 1.091 s vs 22.236 s / 24.473 s. NEGATIVE results in the same table: Ninja is faster at every size (100,000 modules: incremental 10.358 s, null 7.073 s, full 407.131 s vs Bazel 61.911 s, 20.193 s, 1381.402 s), Make run with --no-builtin-rules is also faster than Bazel for incremental and null builds (9.486 s and 7.816 s recursive at 100,000 modules), and Bazel's full build is slower than every Make and Ninja variant (e.g. 82.779 s vs 28.723 s Make and 6.079 s Ninja at 5,000 modules).
compiler_and_flags: No compiler involved (rules touch 0-byte files); tools run with no arguments plus Make with --no-builtin-rules --no-builtin-variables; GNU Make 4.3, Ninja 1.11.1, Bazel 8.0.1 on the Arm runs, Bazel version recorded as 'no_version' on the x86_64 runs.
hardware: x86_64 run: 4 CPUs, 7G RAM, Linux 6.8.0-48-generic (Ubuntu 22.04); Arm run: aarch64 4 CPUs, 7G, Linux 6.8.0-1018-raspi (kernel name suggests a Raspberry Pi); CPU model not stated; runs dated 2025-02-10/11
tradeoffs: JVM server process: 350 to 500 MB resident in these runs and 310 MB to 1 GB of output-base disk even for empty modules; slow cold full build; steep learning curve (BUILD/Starlark files, many options); hermetic sandboxed actions with remote cache and remote execution, whose benefits this benchmark does not exercise. Output lands in the user cache directory, not the source tree.
caveats: The benchmark is synthetic and measures pure build-tool overhead: no compiler runs, so it says nothing about real C or C++ compile and link wall-clock time or about remote caching and execution, which are Bazel's main speed levers. Bazel only wins against Make run with default built-in rules (the benchmark's own results show Make drops to Ninja-like times with --no-builtin-rules) and only on incremental builds from about 5,000 modules and null builds from about 1,000 modules (on Arm at 1,000 modules Make is still faster); at small sizes (50 to 100 modules) Bazel's full build is about 10 to 22 s vs 0.04 to 0.23 s for Ninja and Make, and Ninja beats Bazel in every row. The measurement is by a single maintainer repo with 5 stars (GPL-3.0 benchmark code, last commit 2025-02-28); CPU model is not stated, so it cannot be tier A. The Bazel version is not recorded on the x86_64 runs. The Bazel repo itself carries no Make or Ninja comparison; the Bazel 'fast' claim is first-party and unquantified. [retier] Enricher: one run per cell; the x86 Bazel binary is unstamped (no_version); the disk column is inconsistent (x86 excludes the install base, Arm includes it: 6M vs 310M at 50 modules, 26G vs 341M at 100k); generate.sh deletes the old ~/.cache/bazel with a background rm -rf that overlaps the next tool's timed full build; bazel shutdown is never run between tools.

name: Ninja
baseline: GNU Make (CMake Unix Makefiles generator backend)
workload: Meson author's experiment: 1000 generated trivial C files (each defining one function and including a header) built into one executable with CMake, once with its Make backend and once with its Ninja backend, four parallel processes, fastest of several runs; plus an anecdote about no-op builds of the Clang compiler.
claimed_speedup: Page text: switching the CMake backend from Make to Ninja shaves 3.5 seconds (over 20%) off the total build time of the 1000-file project with no CMake file changes. Chart values (bar-chart PNGs, read off approximately): full build CMake/Make about 16 s vs CMake/Ninja about 12.5 s; empty (no-op) build CMake/Make about 0.55 s vs CMake/Ninja about 0.04 s (about 13x, derived from page data). Page text also says Meson (Ninja backend) takes 0.03 s for the empty build and Autotools, the fastest Make-based system, is almost an order of magnitude slower. Anecdote on the same page: no-op build times of 30 seconds for Make versus less than one second for Ninja when compiling the Clang compiler.
compiler_and_flags: Linked measure.py: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=debug (default Unix Makefiles generator) then make -j 4, versus cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=debug -G Ninja then ninja -j 4; system C compiler picked by CMake (the Meson row sets CC=gcc); compiler, CMake, Make and Ninja versions are not stated.
hardware: 2011-era MacBook Pro running Ubuntu 13.04 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Deliberately has no build-file features (no conditionals, no built-in rules, no globbing); build.ninja files are meant to be emitted by a generator such as CMake or Meson, so Ninja alone is not a replacement for a hand-written Makefile. It needs a generator step. Uses all hardware threads by default; the manual says the design trades convenience for speed.
caveats: The only quantified third-party comparison reachable is written by the author of Meson, a meta-build system that itself generates Ninja files (an interested party for Ninja, competing with CMake rather than with Ninja), and is old (2011-era MacBook Pro, Ubuntu 13.04). CPU model, compiler and tool versions are not stated. The generator and measurement scripts are linked from the page (raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/jpakkane/meson/gen_src.py and measure.py); measure.py times a single build and a single empty build per tool, while the page says the fastest of several runs was taken. The per-tool values are in bar-chart PNGs, so the figures other than the 3.5 s / over 20% text are read off the charts and approximate. The baseline is CMake-generated Makefiles, not a hand-written Makefile, so the gap partly reflects CMake's Makefile generator. The 30 s versus under 1 s Clang figure is explicitly anecdotal. First-party claim on the Ninja manual page (https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja/blob/master/doc/manual.asciidoc, introduction): Chromium, with over 30,000 source files, had other build systems, including one built from custom non-recursive Makefiles, that took ten seconds to start building after changing one file, while Ninja takes under a second; no hardware, date or method is given there, so it is tier C on its own. Ninja's advantage is mostly incremental and no-op startup time; clean full builds are compiler-bound, and the 20 percent gain is on a synthetic project of trivial files, so real projects will see less on clean builds. [retier] Enricher: measure.py does one pass and never cleans the build directories, so the fastest-of-several-runs figures were taken by hand; on the full-build chart Premake's Make backend (about 12.7 s) nearly matches CMake/Ninja (about 12.5 s), so most of the 20% gain over CMake's Makefile generator is generator overhead. In thutt/build-tool-comparator, Make with -rR ties Ninja 1.11.1 on incremental and null builds and beats it on full builds from 50k modules (x86 100k: 103.8 s vs 407.1 s).

name: tup
workload: Synthetic C project generator (logarithmic directory tree, up to 100,000 C files / ~200,000 total files with headers): cold build, single-file-change rebuild, and no-op ('nothing changed') dependency check, tup vs make.
claimed_speedup: At 100k files: no-op check ~0s (tup) vs ~30 minutes (make); single C-file change rebuild ~0.1s (tup) vs ~30 minutes (make). Cold/initial build: tup is 5-30% SLOWER than make across sizes.
tradeoffs: Requires all build outputs declared explicitly (no implicit globbing) for correctness; runs a persistent filesystem-watching 'monitor' process; much smaller ecosystem/IDE support than Make/CMake.
caveats: First-party page with no CPU model, OS or compiler flags stated, and the generator script is not published. The ratio (about 30 min vs 0.1 s) looks implausible, so it is capped at tier C under the >50x rule. The page footer shows a 2008-2024 copyright, so the hardware is likely old. At 100k files the log-scale graphs appear to put make at a little over 1,000 s (about 20 min), which is below the text's 'half an hour'. The near-zero no-op and update times rely on tup's file monitor, which took 9.7 s to start the first time at 200k files and 2 min 30 s with a cold cache (2.5 s hot). The 100k-file case is a stress test, and tup's cold build is 5-30% slower than make.

name: doctest
workload: bench.py-generated CMake projects built single-threaded: (1) 201 source files with the framework header included in every file, (2) 50k CHECK(a==b) asserts across 10 files, (3) a runtime loop of 10 million passing CHECK(i == i) asserts, with and without INFO(i) logging.
claimed_speedup: Header cost: doctest.h costs 11ms-23ms per source file against 380ms-470ms for catch.hpp (page: more than 36 times lighter on MSVC). 201 files with header everywhere, Linux GCC Release: 11.05s vs 99.48s (baselines 4.29s vs 4.50s); MSVC Release: 8.71s vs 87.17s. 50k CHECK(a==b) asserts, Linux GCC Release: 257.40s vs 608.94s; MSVC Release: 58.73s vs 448.68s (page: between 0 and 8 times faster than Catch); with DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS 97.46s on Linux GCC Release. Runtime 10M asserts: MSVC Release 0.40s vs 0.76s, Linux GCC Release 0.29s vs 0.29s, Linux Clang Release 0.28s vs 0.32s; with INFO logging Linux GCC Release 0.52s vs 3.60s (page: around 20% faster for plain asserts, a few times faster with logging).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2017 15.8.1, MinGW-w64 GCC 8.1.0, Linux GCC 6.3.0, Linux Clang 4.0.0. scripts/bench/bench.py configures CMake with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Debug or Release (so CMake's default per-config flags apply: -O3 -DNDEBUG for GCC/Clang Release, /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG for MSVC Release), adds -std=c++11 on non-MSVC and -w on GCC/Clang, and builds single-threaded with cmake --build; scripts/bench/run_all.py averages 3 runs per table cell.
hardware: Intel i7 3770k, 16G RAM; Windows 7 on an SSD, and Ubuntu 17.04 in a VirtualBox VM on a HDD
tradeoffs: Smaller feature set than Catch2 (modelled on Catch; the FAQ lists the differences, not read). The biggest assert-compile wins need the non-decomposing CHECK_EQ(a,b) form and the DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS define, so they are not like-for-like with Catch's CHECK(a==b). DOCTEST_CONFIG_DISABLE strips tests from the binary. Single header, C++11.
caveats: The project's own benchmark (Dec 2018): doctest 2.2.0 against Catch 2.3.0, both far behind current releases; Catch2 v3 became a compiled library with a different compile-time profile and was not measured. Flags come from the public script (CMake build-type defaults) rather than the page text. Linux numbers come from a VirtualBox VM on a HDD. run_all.py at HEAD averages 3 runs per cell, but the page gives no variance, and bench.py has been edited since the 2018 run (a 2019 fix, a 2025 newline/encoding chore, a 2026 cmake_minimum_required bump to 3.14), so a rerun uses a slightly different script. Runtime for plain asserts is near parity on GCC and Clang Release (0.29s vs 0.29s, 0.28s vs 0.32s); the large runtime win is only with INFO logging (the page's 'over 18 times faster' case is MSVC Debug, 11.41s vs 213.91s). README says compile time is better 'by orders of magnitude', while the tables show roughly 9-10x on whole-build header cost and up to about 8x on assert macros (MSVC Release 58.73s vs 448.68s; Linux GCC Release only about 2.4x, derived from page data). Google Test and Boost.Test are not benchmarked on the page. doctest is a unit-testing framework whose speed claim is compile time; it does not cache or distribute builds. name: TinyCC (tcc)
baseline: GCC at -O0 (gcc 16.2.1 in compiler-benchmark, GCC 3.2 in the bellard.org table); also Clang 22.1.8 at -O0
workload: compiler-benchmark default run (--function-count=200 --function-depth=200 --run-count=5). Each repetition writes one generated C file: 40,000 one-line 'long f(long x) { return x + ... + const; }' functions in 200 call chains of depth 200, plus a main that calls the 200 chain heads and returns the sum. There is no #include or other prefix. Times are wall clock (time.perf_counter around subprocess.Popen, with psutil polling every 10 ms at the default --sample-rate=100). Each cell is the minimum of 5 repetitions divided by 40,000 (us per function). Absolute minimums: Build tcc about 0.10 s, clang 2.4 s, gcc 20.0 s; Compile tcc 0.14 s, clang 4.9 s, gcc 29.3 s (derived from page data). bellard.org: the Links browser source, 76,936 lines including headers, of which 1,950,947 lines (67.2 MB) are actually compiled; real time covers compile, assemble and link.
claimed_speedup: nordlow/compiler-benchmark (README table of 2026-09-29, commit 5712a50; per-function minimum of 5 runs over 40,000 generated functions): Build [us/f] tcc 0.9.28rc 2.6 vs gcc 16.2.1 500.7 vs clang 22.1.8 60.3, about 193x faster than gcc -O0 and 23x faster than clang -O0 (derived from page data); Compile [us/f] tcc 3.5 vs gcc 732.5 vs clang 123.3, about 209x and 35x (derived from page data); Check [us/f] tcc 2.9 vs gcc 18.2 vs clang 15.4, about 6.3x and 5.3x (derived from page data), although tcc's Check row does full code generation into /dev/null while gcc and clang only run -fsyntax-only. The previous published run (the table that commit 5712a50 replaced) had Build tcc 3.6 vs gcc 805.8 vs clang 85.3 us/f, about 224x and 24x (derived from page data). First-party bellard.org figure: TinyCC 0.9.22 compiles, assembles and links the Links browser in 2.27 s (859,000 lines/s, 29.6 MB/s) vs GCC 3.2 -O0 in 20.0 s (98,000 lines/s, 3.4 MB/s) on a 2.4 GHz Pentium 4, 'about 9 times faster than GCC' (8.8x, derived from page data). The TinyCC README says 'Compiles and links about 10 times faster than gcc -O0'.
compiler_and_flags: compiler-benchmark script at commit 5712a50, with the same flags at HEAD: gcc 16.2.1 gets -Wall -Wextra; clang 22.1.8 gets -Wall -Wextra -fno-color-diagnostics -fno-caret-diagnostics -fno-diagnostics-show-option. Both then get -fsyntax-only (Check), -c (Compile) or -o main (Build), with no -O flag, so they run at default -O0. tcc 0.9.28rc is a mob-branch snapshot installed as the Arch package by provision.sh; its exact commit is not recorded. It gets -c -o /dev/null (Check), -c (Compile) or -o main (Build), with no warning or optimization flags. All three link in Build (gcc and clang through the system linker, tcc with its built-in linker); none links in Compile. bellard.org: TinyCC 0.9.22 vs GCC 3.2 -O0; no script or flags are published beyond that.
hardware: compiler-benchmark: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350, which the README labels '(8+8) @ 5.09 GHz'. It is a 28 W Krackan Point laptop part with 4 Zen 5 cores (up to 5.0 GHz) and 4 Zen 5c cores (up to 3.5 GHz), 16 threads. Arch Linux; the README says 'as of 2026-09' and the table was committed on 2026-09-29 (5712a50). bellard.org: 2.4 GHz Pentium 4 (TinyCC 0.9.22 was tagged 2004-11-08; GCC 3.2 dates from 2002).
stars_or_usage: About 3.0k stars and 570 forks on the GitHub mirror (github.com showed 3,000 on 2026-10-07; 3038 at the 2026-09-24 check). The mirror describes itself as an 'Unofficial mirror of mob development branch' of repo.or.cz/tinycc.git. The V language bundles TCC binaries for fast development builds.
tradeoffs: Single-pass compiler with no optimizer: generated code is unoptimized (similar to gcc -O0), so it suits compile-and-run scripting, bootstrapping and fast edit cycles but not performance-critical builds. Supports i386, x86_64, arm, aarch64, riscv64 and has an optional bounds checker. Does not support C++.
caveats: The benchmark is synthetic (one huge TU of arithmetic call chains, no #include or header parsing); its own README says real-world build times are dominated by headers and linking, so the ~190x gap overstates typical gains (the project claims about 10x vs gcc -O0, and a 2003-era Links browser comparison of 2.27 s vs 20.0 s on GCC 3.2 appears only in search snippets because bellard.org was blocked). gcc and clang are compared at their default -O0, not at -O2, so the win is against unoptimized builds only. In this run the produced binaries' run time was 113 us/f for tcc vs 98 for gcc and 155 for clang, but run time is measured on the same synthetic code. The benchmark author is a third party (nordlow), but the suite is a single-maintainer repo with 166 stars; the tcc check row uses -c so it also emits object code unlike gcc -fsyntax-only. License: COPYING is LGPL-2.1; a RELICENSING file lists authors agreeing to MIT-style terms, but the whole tree is not relicensed. [retier] This supersedes the earlier note that a gcc -O0 baseline caps the entry at C. The tier now rests on a public third-party harness, with -O0 recorded as a caveat. The workload is synthetic: a single translation unit of arithmetic call chains with no #include. The benchmark README itself warns that real-world build times are 'heavily driven by header parsing (#include), package/module resolution, standard library footprint, and cross-crate/module parallelism, none of which are exercised by isolated arithmetic trees'. gcc and clang run at their default -O0 (plus -Wall -Wextra, which tcc does not get), so the lead holds only against unoptimized builds. The 193x Build gap over gcc is about 20x TinyCC's own 'about 10 times faster than gcc -O0' claim. It comes almost entirely from gcc's code generation on this one huge translation unit: gcc Check 18.2 vs Compile 732.5 us/f (derived from page data). The same Check-to-Compile jump does not appear in the bellard.org multi-file 8.8x. tcc's Check row emits code into /dev/null, while gcc and clang only run -fsyntax-only. The harness is noisy. In the 2026-09-29 table Build is lower than Compile for all three compilers (gcc 500.7 vs 732.5, clang 60.3 vs 123.3, tcc 2.6 vs 3.5 us/f), even though Build does strictly more work. Between the two published runs, clang Compile moved from 83.5 to 123.3 (+48%) and gcc Build from 805.8 to 500.7 (-38%) (derived from page data). At commit 5712a50 the script ran len(cpus)-2 tasks at once (14 on this 16-thread part), each pinned by worker index to one logical CPU, on a 28 W laptop chip that mixes 5.0 GHz Zen 5 and 3.5 GHz Zen 5c cores. Pinning to performance cores only arrived in a 2026-10-06 commit, after this run. The tcc-vs-clang Build ratio still stays at 23-24x across both runs. Polling every 10 ms adds up to about 10% to tcc's roughly 0.10 s builds but almost nothing to gcc's 20 s builds, so it understates tcc's lead. tcc's output is not validated. The harness checks only the compiler exit code and stderr, and it runs each built binary 5 times with output discarded, never checking its exit status or sum. Run time is reported only as speed: tcc 113 vs gcc -O0 98 vs clang -O0 155 us/f, with nothing at -O2. The exact tcc mob commit is not recorded; the table shows only 0.9.28rc. The script has changed since the run (work directory moved to /tmp, core selection, table layout), so reproducing the table needs the script at commit 5712a50. compiler-benchmark is a single-maintainer repo (nordlow, 166 stars, MIT). The bellard.org 8.8x figure is first-party, has no published script, and uses TinyCC 0.9.22 against GCC 3.2 -O0 on a Pentium 4. bellard.org was EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so the figure was re-confirmed from a search snippet and the 2026-09-24 verifier's reading. The GitHub repo is an unofficial mirror of the repo.or.cz mob branch. The last tagged release is release_0_9_27 (2017-12-12), and mob's VERSION reads 0.9.28rc, so the measured code is available only from mob, not from a release. COPYING is LGPL-2.1 and the README says TCC is distributed under the LGPL. A RELICENSING file lists authors who agree to MIT-style terms for their own contributions; it does not relicense the whole tree.
